messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Sex: Sex, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malia was nineteen years old, a fisherman working the docks alongside her father and older brother in a small coastal town. She had been on the water since she was a child, and the rhythm of the boat, the slap of lines, the low drone of the engine—these were the sounds of safety. That changed on a late autumn afternoon when a sudden squall rolled in without warning. The sea turned grey and violent, and as her father struggled to haul in a snarled net, a loose winch cable whipped across the deck. Malia saw her brother lunge to push their father out of the way. The cable caught him across the chest. He was dead before he hit the water.

In the months that followed, Malia did not stop working. She worked longer hours than anyone else on the dock, taking extra shifts, staying out after dark. She told herself it was to help her father, who had become hollow and quiet, but the real reason was simpler: when she was working, she did not have to be alone with what was inside her head. The moment she stopped, the memory would force its way in—not as a clear picture, but as a wave of raw, full-intensity terror that came without warning and without an image. She would feel the same helpless horror she had felt on the deck, but her mind would be blank, and she would be left gasping, unable to explain to anyone why she had suddenly frozen or started shaking.

She had also stopped letting her boyfriend touch her. Sex was out of the question. The thought of being that vulnerable, of losing control of her body in any way, made her skin crawl. She spent her evenings on her phone, scrolling through videos and games for hours, until her eyes burned and she could barely keep them open. It was the only way to keep the thoughts at bay until she was exhausted enough to sleep.

What frightened her most, though, was a growing conviction that she was dangerous. She had come to believe that she could not control her own anger, that if she ever let it out she would do something terrible. She had never been a violent person, but now she avoided any situation that might frustrate her. When a delivery was late or a piece of gear jammed, her heart would pound and she would assume something catastrophic was happening—a boat sinking, a man overboard. Her body would react before her mind had time to think, and she would find herself already in a cold sweat, scanning the horizon for a threat that was not there. She had begun to feel betrayed by her own body. It kept reacting as if she were still in danger, even when she was standing safely on the dock in broad daylight.

The guilt was the worst part. She was certain she should have protected her brother. She had been right there, only a few feet away. She replayed the moment again and again, trying to find a version where she could have done something different, but there was nothing. The memory came when it wanted, uninvited, and each time she felt the same crushing guilt, as fresh as if it had just happened.

It was her boyfriend who finally convinced her to come in. He had found her one night on the bathroom floor, shaking, unable to say what was wrong because there was no image to describe—only the feeling, the full weight of that afternoon pressing down on her chest. She came because she was afraid of what she might become if she kept going like this. She was afraid of the anger she could feel building, and afraid that one day she would not be able to hold it back. She was hoping, more than anything, to feel safe in her own body again.
